worker_notes: Identity assessment: supplied text is a full primary journal article (17 numbered pages, methods/results, appendix and references), not an abstract or secondary report. First-page title is The Affect Heuristic in Judgments of Risks and Benefits (with encoding artifacts); authors Melissa L. Finucane, Ali Alhakami, Paul Slovic and Stephen M. Johnson match the supplied reference. Journal header gives Journal of Behavioral Decision Making 13: 1–17 (2000); repeated Wiley download footer identifies DOI 10.1002/(SICI)1099-0771(200001/03)13:1<1::AID-BDM333>3.0.CO;2-S, matching the assigned original. No PDF was supplied. Target matched by Study 2, p. 11 and the explicit risk/benefit relationship, not numeric matching or row order. The canonical text encodes the negative sign as ÿ; es.value transcribes the negative correlation as -0.75 without conversion. The correlation concerns aggregate t-values, not a participant-level correlation. No p is printed for this correlation in its paragraph, Exhibit 6 caption, or continuation of Study 2 results. The nearby p bounds (canonical text p 5 0.01) concern nuclear-power pre/post t tests and cannot be assigned to the correlation. N, replication and reported_success are unassigned placeholders; no analytic N is derived or extracted.

coding_context.description: increasing benefits leads people to judge its risks as lower
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
In two well-powered studies, using a more stringent analytic strategy, we
replicated the original finding. We observed a strong negative relationship between judgments of risks and benefits across
three technologies, although we do find that there was no change in risks when highlighting low benefits.
